s16.slug: SUNDAY · 11:30 AM · ST. BRENDAN THE NAVIGATOR — THE 11:30
body: The 11:30 is the families’ Mass, the sunburned one: strollers parked in the side aisle, little boys in clip-on ties, surfers in the back pews with their hair still wet from the morning. Last week the 9:30 was Lena’s, and Kenzie cantors it. The 11:30 has a guitar choir instead, four guitars and a tambourine in the corner under the window where St. Brendan is crossing the sea in a boat made of leather, and all four guitars are tuning to a slightly different idea of the same note.

It was Skye’s idea. She picked him up at ten past eleven in a dress he has never seen — navy, with small white dots, sleeves to the elbow — with a cardigan over her arm because somebody had told her churches are cold, and her hair pinned back off her face with what looked like research. She looked at his tie when he got in.
“It’s crooked,” she said. “Keep it. It reads as sincere.” And then, pulling away from the curb: “Yesterday was the street. I want to see the inside.”

Inside, she does what he does. Not a performance of it; she follows. At the font he dips his fingers and she dips hers after him and touches her forehead and stops there, not sure where it goes next, so he does the rest of it slower than he has done it since the second grade — forehead, chest, left shoulder, right — and she finishes it a half-beat behind him. At the end of the pew he genuflects and she goes down beside him on one knee in the dotted dress, carefully, a girl curtsying to somebody she’s been warned about. At the opening hymn he stands a little late so she can see him stand; when it’s time to sit, he sits a little late. He goes through the Mass at the speed of somebody who has never been to one, so she can keep up with him, and by the Gloria he’s seeing it at that speed too: the candles, the green on the altar, the old woman in front of them with a rosary wound through her fingers and her eyes shut, a little boy asleep across his father’s lap with his mouth open.

A woman from the parish council reads Nehemiah, in a blazer with a Haiti ribbon on the lapel. Ezra the priest stands up on a wooden platform and reads the law to the people of Jerusalem from daybreak till noon, and the people stand and listen to it, and they weep. And Ezra and the governor tell them to stop. Go home, eat rich food, drink something sweet, send a portion to whoever has nothing; this day is holy.
“*Do not be saddened this day,*” the lector reads, “*for rejoicing in the LORD must be your strength!*”

Skye has sat forward at the weeping. She has sat through more table reads than anyone in this church, and she sits forward at a crowd crying at one, interested, a professional at somebody else’s scene.

The choir does the psalm. A teenage boy reads Corinthians — the body, and its parts, the foot that says it isn’t a hand — with his voice cracking halfway down the page. Osei comes to the ambo for the Gospel himself, in the green, favoring the leg, and begins at the beginning of Luke, where Luke says he has decided to write it all down in order for somebody called Theophilus.
Skye turns her head an inch and mouths it at him: *Ted?*
He keeps his face straight. It costs him.

Osei reads on. Nazareth, the synagogue on the sabbath, the scroll of Isaiah handed up to Jesus; he finds the place and reads it, and rolls it up, and gives it back to the attendant, and sits down, and every eye in the room is on him.
“*Today this Scripture passage is fulfilled in your hearing.*”
Osei doesn’t come down the step this time. He stays at the ambo with both hands on it.
“The hardest word in this Gospel is not *Scripture*, and it is not *fulfilled*,” he says. “It is *today*. Not the day you will be ready for — this one, with whatever you have brought into it.”
And he sits down, and lets the church be quiet, and somewhere in the back the little boy wakes up and says *What?* to his father, and half the church hears it, and nobody laughs except the father.

Before the offertory Osei stands again. “The second collection is for Haiti,” he says. “The bishops ask it of every parish in the country this weekend, and I ask it of you.” Skye opens her purse and takes out a plain white envelope, already sealed. She brought it. She read ahead. When the long-handled basket comes down their pew she puts it in herself, and holds it a second over the basket before she lets go.
“This one’s me,” she says, low, to nobody but him.

At the Lamb of God the pews begin to empty forward from the front. The old woman in front of them goes, and the sleeping boy’s father with the boy over his shoulder, and the surfers from the back go past their row smelling of neoprene. Jack kneels.

He doesn’t go up. He knew he wouldn’t when he put the tie on. He shuts his eyes and starts the one Nonna taught him at the kitchen table for the Sundays you can’t, and keeps going under the guitars to the end. *My Jesus, I believe that You are present in the Most Holy Sacrament.* The line goes past the end of the pew in its good shoes. *Since I cannot at this moment receive You sacramentally, come at least spiritually into my heart.*

Beside him the kneeler creaks. Skye had half stood with everyone else, and sat back down when he didn’t, and now she kneels too, a half-beat after him, because that’s what they’re doing today. She doesn’t know the rule. She doesn’t need the rule to know him. She tips her head toward his until her temple is nearly at his ear.
“Are we in trouble?” she whispers.
He shakes his head at the floor: a lie about the size a man tells in church. She lets him have it, for now, and stays on her knees beside him until the line comes back.
Afterward Osei is on the front steps in the noon sun in his vestments, shaking every hand that comes out of the door, children included. Jack waits their turn.
“Father,” he says, “this is Skye.”
“Skye,” Osei says.
He says it like any name, and takes her hand in both of his, and Jack knows exactly where Osei has heard that name before, and that it will stay there.
“Welcome,” Osei says.

Skye says thank you, and that she liked the part about *today*, and Osei says he will tell the man who wrote it. While she is turning to go down the steps, he holds Jack’s hand a moment longer, and says it quietly, not as a reproach — as a fact on a schedule.
“Wednesday. Eight o’clock.”
And he turns to the family behind them, five of them, and has all five of their names.

journal.title: Fr. Gabriel Osei
journal.text: Newman chaplain. Kumasi, Ghana. Used to be a doctor. Limps and doesn’t mention it. Plays chess like he’s got all night and highlife like the neighbors owe him money. Told me a proverb about funerals. I laughed. That was apparently the point. Said Nonna’s Mass himself at the 12:10, like he promised. Gave me a card for her: ‘A grandmother likes paper.’ Blessed Hale’s deaf dog with his hand on its ribs, where it could hear. Finished Hale’s limerick for him. Laughed for a full minute at Becca’s crab. All Souls, at the book: ‘Write them all. He has a large book and a long memory.’ Saturday, behind the screen, one question: do I want to stop seeing her, or stop what happens. Change the hour. Keep her in the daylight. The Advent party: got the spray tan. Confiscated the mistletoe — he requested. At the sink he told me about the waiting room in Kumasi. His door is the one with the light on. Saturday, behind the screen: love wills the good of the other — and that’s why it’s dangerous. Gaudete: rejoice is a command. Wednesday, behind the screen: I’m not avoiding the occasion, I’m scheduling it. Distance is a mercy; use it. Blessed us both for the road on the Newman steps. Come back. The first day back I gave him Father Dom’s message: we’ll see. He laughed. I told him I went at home. The night of the earthquake he asked the bishop if he could spare an old doctor. The bishop couldn’t spare a young priest. His friend Yaw from medical school is in Port-au-Prince — alive, operating in a parking lot. Saturday at three-thirty the light was on. Sunday he read Cana. Yaw has a generator now. Sunday at the 11:30 I didn’t go up. At the door I introduced him to Skye. He said her name. Then he said Wednesday, eight o’clock.

s16a.slug: SUNDAY · 12:35 PM · OCEAN ROAD, THE SAAB, TOP DOWN
body: She puts the top down in the lot for the first warm noon of the year, and drives down Ocean Road one-handed with the cardigan thrown in the back seat and the church getting smaller in the mirror — the olive tree over the courtyard wall, the bell tower white against the hills. She doesn’t put the iPod on. She hasn’t said anything since the steps, and she drives the first quarter mile in it, with her elbow on the door and her hair coming loose from the pins one strand at a time. Twice she starts to say something and turns it into a lane change. A man with a longboard under his arm crosses in front of them at the crosswalk by the liquor store, in flip-flops on the warm asphalt, and she waits for him with the patience of somebody who has a question saved.
At the light at Las Olas she stops, and puts both hands on the wheel, and turns in her seat and looks at him.
“Everybody went up,” she says. “The surfers went up. The little boy who said *what*. You knelt.” She doesn’t make it a bit. “Why didn’t you go up?”
She asks it the way she asks the things she actually wants to know: straight, at a red light, with forty seconds of nowhere to go for either of them.

choices.text: “Because of Friday. I’m not going to lie to you about that.”
choices.key: You told Skye why you stayed in the pew.
response: He says it straight back, at the same red light, before the forty seconds are up.

The light goes green. She doesn’t go. She sits with both hands on the wheel, looking at him, and he lets her look; there’s nothing in his face he’s going to move out of the way. The car behind them waits a decent interval for a Sunday, and then honks.
She puts it in gear. She drives exactly as far as the turnout above the water, a few hundred yards down on the ocean side, and pulls onto the gravel, and turns the engine off.

choices.text: *Explain it properly — Communion, confession, all of it.*
choices.key: You told Skye why you stayed in the pew, and what it means.
response: He tries to do it properly, from the beginning, and does it badly and in order.

That what goes up the aisle isn’t bread to him, or a reminder, or a symbol of anything; it’s Him, and that’s the claim, and he knows how it sounds. That you don’t take that into your mouth with something serious on you that you haven’t confessed. What makes it serious: that it’s grave, and you knew, and you chose it anyway. What confession is for. The closet at the back of the church, the screen, the words.

The light goes green halfway through and she drives through it without taking her eyes off the road for longer than it takes to ask the next one. Who decides what’s grave? Out loud, every time? Does the priest know it’s you? Does he remember? She asks them like homework she picked herself, and he answers what he can, and twice he says *I don’t know* and she nods as if that counts too. She’s going to read about it tonight, she says. She reads ahead.
And it gets where it was always going. Grave, and knowing, and choosing it.
“Friday,” she says.
“Friday.”
She pulls into the turnout above the water and turns the engine off.

choices.key: You made a joke, and then told Skye why you stayed in the pew.
response: “Long story,” he says. “Two thousand years.”
“I have two thousand years.” She doesn’t take her eyes off him. The light is still red, and she’s not looking at it. “Start at Friday.”

So he does. He starts at Friday, at the light at Las Olas, and when it goes green she pulls through the intersection and straight into the turnout on the far side above the water, and turns the engine off, and he’s still talking, and it still comes out to the same place: because of Friday.

choices.key: You tried to put it off, and then told Skye why you stayed in the pew.
response: “Ask me tonight,” he says.

She doesn’t let him. The light goes green and she drives through it, and a few hundred yards down she puts her blinker on and pulls into the next turnout above the water, onto the gravel, and stops. She leaves the engine running. She doesn’t say anything. Her right thumb starts on the wheel, along the stitching, back and forth.
He watches the thumb go. She would sit here till dark.
“Because of Friday,” he says.
The thumb stops. She turns the key, and the engine dies, and the sea comes up the bluff to fill in where it was.

s16b.slug: SUNDAY · 12:41 PM · THE TURNOUT ABOVE THE WATER → SEACLIFF ROAD
body: The turnout is a gravel shelf on the ocean side of the road with a trash can chained to a post, and below it the bluff goes down in ice plant to the sand, and the Channel lies out there flat and blue to the islands. A pelican goes along the face of the bluff at eye level without moving its wings.
Skye has her hands in her lap. She’s looking at the water. He has seen her do this with pages handed to her in a car: going through it once for the sense, before she decides how to play it.
“So it’s a sin to you,” she says. “Friday.”
“Yes.”
She nods at the water. It isn’t hurt, or not in any way he could put his finger on, and it isn’t a laugh. She works at it.
“So you go in,” she says, “and you tell him, and he says the words, and it’s — what. Cut. Back to one. Like it never shot.”
“It still happened. It’s forgiven. That’s different.”

“I’ve had a board of directors on my body since I was a kid.” Her voice stays even. “The network. My mother. A man with a tape measure. You were the one person I’d met who didn’t have a note on it.” She looks down at her hands. “And it turns out you do. It’s just from higher up.”
He turns in his seat so she has to look at him or look away on purpose.
“You’re not what I confess,” he says. “What I did is.”

The pelican has gone. Down on the sand a man is throwing a tennis ball into the shore break for a black dog that keeps bringing it back. She looks at him, closer than a red light, and then she asks the real one, the one under all of it.
“Are you sorry?”
He could make this easy. He can see the easy version from here. He doesn’t want her to have the easy version.
“I’m sorry for what I did,” he says. “I’m not sorry it was you.”
“That,” Skye says, “is a terrible apology.”
“It wasn’t one. You asked if I was sorry.”

Her mouth goes at one corner, and doesn’t get any further than that. Whatever it costs to sit in a car and hear both of those from a boy who won’t pretend either one away, she sits there and pays it. It costs him to say them to her face in daylight, with nothing to look at but the sea. Neither of them gets out of the car.
“Wednesday at eight,” he says. “I’ll go and tell a priest. Next Sunday I go up.”

That’s his plan, and it’s all of it. She takes it without arguing. She reaches over instead and gets her fingers into the knot of his tie, the crooked one she told him to keep, and works it loose, and pulls it out from under his collar in one long zip of silk and drops it in the back seat on top of her cardigan.
“Church is over,” she says.

She backs out onto Ocean Road. She takes the long curve down toward Seacliff without a word, with the wind in her hair and the pins giving up all at once, and he watches her think the whole length of the curve. At the bottom of it the light at Seacliff is red again, and she brakes, and puts both hands up on top of the wheel.
“I’m *starving*,” she announces, to the entire coast. “I could eat a Viking.”

s17.slug: SUNDAY · 12:50 PM · LUPE’S TRUCK, THE HEAD OF SEACLIFF ROAD
body: Carnitas and diesel and the sea: Lupe’s white truck is parked at the head of Seacliff in broad daylight with the generator going and the chile lights off, and half a dozen surfers in wetsuits peeled to the waist are standing around the window holding paper boats. On Sundays when the Point is open Lupe sets up here at noon for the surfers; nights, she’s where she always is. Jack has never seen the truck by sun. It looks smaller in it, and cleaner, and more like a business.
Lupe knows him from two in the morning. She leans out of the window and looks at him in the noon light, gold tooth and all, checking the face against the one she has on file.
“Daylight,” she says. “*Qué milagro.*”

They eat off the hood of the Saab in the sun, carnitas and the green salsa and the radishes, the metal warm through Skye’s dress where she’s leaning on it. Lupe has the Jets and the Colts going on the dash radio, low, and Skye asks her who she’s got today, like a bettor at a window.

Lupe has opinions about the Vikings. The Vikings, Lupe says, have a grandfather at quarterback. Forty years old. A grandfather is wonderful all day, she says, and at the end he gives it away to the other team, because he loves everybody. “My father at forty,” Lupe says, “could not find the truck.”

“Then I’m with the other ones,” Skye says. She has done the reading. She informs Lupe that the Vikings are the purple ones with horns on their helmets, which she respects as a choice; that the Saints are the gold ones with the — she draws it in the air with a radish and can’t find the word — the lily; and that the team on the radio right now are horses, from Indiana, which she finds sweet. “Wikipedia,” she tells Jack, when he looks over. “Three hours. I took notes.” Her Rite Aid scarf is in the back seat, black and gold, folded under his tie, ready to go.

And she does the Who Dat for Lupe, right there at the window, phonetically, with both fists, as Joey and Dale taught her, with Joey’s coaster somewhere in the bottom of her purse in case she forgets. Two of the surfers do it back at her, badly, out of politeness or Louisiana. Lupe applauds with the tongs.
A silver Corolla with a St. Brendan’s lot sticker in the back window slows on Seacliff as it passes the truck, and goes on toward Mission.

At one o’clock by the dash clock Skye holds her hand out to him palm up, carnitas in the other. “Phones,” she says. “It’s a closed set.” His RAZR goes into the glove box on top of her white one, and she snaps it shut on both of them with her knee.
She licks salsa off her thumb and turns to him with her face lit up, flushed from the chant.
“What time’s kickoff?” she says. “I’ve been practicing.”
He isn’t going, and she doesn’t know it yet.

choices.text: “I’m not going. They said things about you, and I’m still mad. I’d rather be with you.”
choices.cue: Skye heard what you didn’t say.
choices.key: You skipped the Saints and told Skye why: you’re angry at Laney and Lena for what they said about her.
response: “I’m not going,” he says. “They said things about you, and I’m still mad.”

She waits for the rest of it, so he tells her the rest. Laney at the table last Saturday — she was there; she heard it. Lena, after, in the back hall, something he isn’t going to repeat to her face. And yesterday at the van. He doesn’t want to sit in that room for four hours and be polite about any of it. “I’d rather be with you.”

Skye watches him over the paper boat. She stays a little longer on *mad* than on the rest of it, testing its weight like a line somebody else wrote. What was said at the van she leaves where it is. She doesn’t say a name.
“Okay,” she says, too brightly — a yes with every light up and nobody behind it.
He puts his plate down on the hood.
“It’s not a sacrifice,” he says. “I want the day.”
Something in her face clears, like the Channel when the wind drops. She picks his plate back up and puts it in his hands, and steals a radish off it.

choices.text: “I’m boycotting. It’s a principled position. There’s carnitas.”
choices.key: You called it a boycott, and then told Skye the truth: you’re angry at Laney and Lena for what they said about her.
response: “I’m boycotting,” he says. “It’s a principled position. There’s carnitas.”
Skye laughs with her mouth full, and has to put a hand up over it, and Lupe looks out of the window to see what’s funny.

He tells her the reason anyway, because it’s hers to have. That he’s angry. Laney last Saturday — she heard that one herself. Lena, after, in the back hall, something he’s not going to say to her on the hood of a car. And yesterday at the van. He doesn’t want to spend four hours in that room being civil about it. He’d rather do something else. With her.
She listens to every word. At *angry* she stops, and turns that one over longer than the others — he can see her do it — and she leaves it where he put it, and leaves the van alone.
“Okay,” she says, too brightly, a soundstage bright, and nobody home.
He catches her wrist on the way to another radish, before it can be the end of the subject.
“It’s not a sacrifice,” he says. “I want the day.”
Her face clears. She takes the radish anyway, with the hand he isn’t holding, and eats it at him.

choices.text: *Tell her what Sully’s was, before, and why you’re giving it up.*
choices.key: You told Skye what Sully’s was to you, and that you’re giving it up because of what Laney and Lena said about her.
response: He tells her what Sully’s was. Every Saints game since September, the long table, the same faces. Dale at the end of the bar with his root beer, explaining punting to anybody who’ll stand still. He has never been to New Orleans and he knows the chant. It was his Sundays. It isn’t now.

And the reason. That he’s angry — at Laney, last Saturday; she heard it. At Lena, after, in the back hall, for something he isn’t going to repeat to her. At yesterday at the van. That he doesn’t want to sit in that room and be polite about it, and he’d rather spend the day with her than spend it there.
Skye listens with the paper boat forgotten in her hand. She stays on *angry* a moment longer than the rest, he watches her stay on it, and the van she leaves alone.
“Okay,” she says, too brightly — a girl to a producer who has just told her the part went another way.
He takes the paper boat out of her hand and sets it on the hood, so she has to look at him.
“It’s not a sacrifice,” he says. “I want the day.”
And something in her face clears. She reaches past him for the boat and eats the last of the carnitas out of it with her fingers, as if somebody might take that away too.

s18.slug: SUNDAY · 1:40 PM · MARISOL POINT, THE DIRT LOT → THE INSIDE
body: She produces the afternoon. She does it from the driver’s seat in the dirt lot at the end of Seacliff with the engine off, ticking items off on her fingers: call time is now. Wardrobe is Tomás’s spare suit, which lives in the trunk and has opinions. Craft services is what’s left of the carnitas. Talent will attempt a three-second stand-up; if talent falls over, they’ll fix it in post. Wrap is when nobody can feel their feet. “Any questions,” she says. “No. Good. Great meeting.”

Tomás is in the lot already, waxing his board on the tailgate of the van with his wetsuit tied around his waist by the arms. He looks up at the two of them getting out of the Saab and takes it all in, the dotted dress and the shirt with no tie, and delivers his news.
“Point’s open, bro.”
*tomas says the point might open sunday*, her text said Thursday night. Tomás was right.

From the edge of the lot it’s all there again. The lines come walking in out of the west, long and even, a little apart from each other like people who don’t know each other in a line at the bank, and every one of them bends as it crosses the reef and wraps in toward the same rocks and peels off them, one after another, breaking where it does. Five or six men in black suits are already sitting out past the reef. Skye stands beside him in her dress with her arms folded, watching it with the face she had for Conan.
“There,” she says. “Where it does.”

Up the bluff, at the end of the low wall, there’s the white cross, and at the foot of it there are flowers again. Roses from a supermarket, red, still in their cellophane, tied to the post with new string. The storm took the last ones and left a length of string standing out sideways in the wind; somebody has been since.
“Somebody’s not sad Sunday,” Skye says.
Jack looks up at the crossbar, at the name painted there, and down at the roses, and then she has him by the sleeve and they’re going back to the trunk.
They change by the open doors of the Saab. She has her suit on and zipped before he has worked out which end of Tomás’s is the legs. He points out that it’s two in the afternoon.
“You owe me a Saturday,” she says, and puts her knee in his back and zips him up. “I’m taking a Sunday. Afternoon’s just weather. You’re not ready for honest.”

They go in on the inside, south of the reef, where the white water runs in over the sand bar in low broken lines, and nowhere near the men at the Point. He is still very bad at it. He falls off the front, and off the back, and once off the side in a way she says she has never seen anybody do and would like him to do again, slower. He gets sand in Tomás’s suit to the knees. He swallows a good part of the Channel.

And then, on a little line that comes in clean, he gets his knees under him, and a foot, and the other foot, and he’s up. One. The board running in straight on the white water with him on it, arms out, knees bent. Two. No kind of surfer at all, upright, the sun on the water in front of him in pieces. Three. The nose catches, and the Pacific takes the board away from him like a parent taking a pair of scissors.

When he comes up, coughing, she isn’t screaming. She is twenty yards out, sitting up on her board with her legs hanging down in the water and her hair slicked back, and she’s looking at him. She has nothing to film with, and wouldn’t.
He paddles out to her. Quiet, from her, means come here.

journal.title: Oceanography 1
journal.text: Oceanography 1, Tuesdays and Thursdays at eleven, Morro Hall 1100. Rocks for Jocks, Wet. Skye took it too and didn’t tell me which science till she was sitting in the back row under the exit sign with the book. Fenner: seventy-one percent, and we have better maps of Mars. The ground is not where you left it, week two. Partners by seat, Thursday. Skye, till May. No trades. Our project is the Point — why it breaks where it does. Fenner: approved, don’t drown. Tuesday: half of Pair 41. Wednesday: field data from the lot in a storm — it wasn’t breaking where it does. It was breaking everywhere. Sunday: the Point open again — breaking where it does.

s18b.slug: SUNDAY · 3:40 PM · MARISOL POINT, OUTSIDE THE WHITE WATER
body: Out past the white water they sit on the boards side by side with their feet hanging down in the Channel, and the swell comes under them in long slow breaths and lifts them and sets them down. She tells him what he looked like. She does the arms. She does his face, which was apparently the face of a man reading his own name on a list he never signed. The sun has gone lower over the islands, and he doesn’t know what time it is. There isn’t a clock anywhere in the water.

body.text: Last night, in the car, he said daylight. There isn’t going to be more daylight than this.
body.else: Yesterday at the curb she got out of the car and stood next to him and didn’t ask. Wednesday at the turnout she asked once, and let it go. Both times she let him keep it. He is tired of keeping it.

body: “Wednesday,” he says. “At the turnout, in the rain. You asked me what happened Tuesday, and I didn’t say anything.”
She doesn’t turn her head. One of her hands is trailing in the water, and it stops trailing.

“I didn’t say anything because I don’t know,” he says. “That’s the true answer. I don’t know what happened. Laney came down to the laundry room in the storm to say some things, and I said some things back, loud, and I slammed the lid of a dryer. And she stopped. In the middle. She looked at me like I’d changed the channel, and she went upstairs.” A swell lifts them and puts them down. “And since then she doesn’t hate me. She hated me for five months, and she was good at it — she was *committed* — and now she says my last name like it’s the weather and leaves granola bars on my tray. And Theo’s doing bits with her in the Commons. About *listening*. They have blocking. I don’t know what any of it is. Ask Theo and you get a bit.”

All of that is true, and it isn’t all of it. What he said with the dryer lid up stays down there in the basement. He watches her find the edge of it: her eyes come to his mouth and stay there a second, where the rest would come out if it were coming, and go back to the water. She doesn’t ask what he said.
“But here’s the part that’s mine,” he says. “You said I was funnier on the phone than I’ve ever been in my life. From the bus shelter.”
“You were. It was upsetting.”
“That wasn’t Laney. Whatever Laney’s thing is, that wasn’t it.” He gets his hands flat on the deck of the board, because they want something to do. “I decided something.”
Now she turns her head.

Over break, he tells her, Nonna asked him a question, and Danny asked him one, the same week, at two different tables, and neither of them knew about the other one. Neither of them really knew about her yet, either, so they were general questions — the kind people in his family ask you instead of *how are you*. Danny, across a table in the visiting room at Trumbull, asked him who out here he could tell the truth to. Nonna asked him on Christmas night, over her beads, in Italian, and it’s better in Italian, and in English it comes out something like who makes him pray.

“I’ve been carrying them around since I got back,” he says. “Turning them over. Every day.” He looks out at the reef, at the next line bending in. “And after the basement I knew. Walking up to the bus shelter in the rain, I knew. It’s you. Both of them. It’s you.”
The swell lifts them, and sets them down.
“So I called you, and I was funny,” he says. “Because I was happy. I’m as happy as I’ve ever been in my life, Skye. That’s what you heard.”

She looks at him across the two boards for a long time. She’s too good a reader not to find the seams — the basement he walked her around the edge of, the place where he translated his grandmother a little loosely — and he watches her find them, one and then the other. Then he watches her set them down. What she’s holding is true, and she can tell it’s true the way she can tell a real line from a learned one: he decided something, and it was her, and the boy on the phone in the bus shelter was happy, and is. The girl who always lands the button doesn’t have one. Her eyes fill, and she lets them, and doesn’t make the joke about the salt.

She reaches across the water and gets hold of the rail of his board, and pulls it in, hand over hand, until the noses knock and her knee is against his and the next swell lifts the two of them at once, like one thing.
“Both,” she says.
“Both.”
She puts her forehead against his. Her hair is cold and her forehead is warm. “There’s more,” she says — not asking. Letting him know she knows. “In the basement. In the questions.”
“Some,” he says. “You’re the part I’m sure of.”
She thinks about that for the length of one swell, going up and coming down.

“That’s enough,” she says, and it is; he can hear her mean it. She kisses him with the Pacific on both their mouths, sitting up on two boards in the open water, and the boards try to drift apart under them, and she holds his on with one hand and doesn’t let it.
Behind them the next line is already bending in around the reef.

s18a.slug: SUNDAY · 5:20 PM · DEL PLAYA LANE, THE PORCH WITH NO SWING
body: The sun went into the Channel at a quarter past five, red, flattening at the bottom where it touched, and what it left behind is going orange over the islands and then green and then nothing at all. The porch has its two bare hooks and its swaying length of chain. Against the rail leans the seat of a new swing, Sol’s, a plank of driftwood she has been sanding pale all week, with a coffee can of screws beside it. Through the screen door Tomás’s stereo is playing something with guitars and a lot of men singing in harmony, like a choir that lives in the woods.

Jack and Skye are on the top step under one blanket, his hair stiff with salt, her feet in his lap, both of them still faintly sore all over from the water. Sol is inside. Tomás comes out when the record ends and sets a paint-spattered radio on the porch rail and turns the dial through static until he finds the game, and turns it down low, and goes back in.

It’s on all evening, at the edge of things. A man’s voice talking fast and low, a crowd behind it like surf. Three doors down Del Playa a house party with its windows open groans and shouts at things none of them can see, and the street has its own weather from it, a groan that goes along the block and dies, a cheer that doesn’t. Jack doesn’t ask the score. Skye doesn’t tell him.

“Do you want to know what I’m afraid of?” she says, when the light has gone. She doesn’t wait. “Sharks, a little, still. Live television. Being the nice one until I’m forty.” She pulls the blanket up. “That I’m a phase.”
He waits.

“You decided. I believe you. I watched you mean it.” Her voice has gone flat. “And people get better at God. One day you look back at a girl in a Saab and think, that was my wild year. Good for her. She was very nice to me.”

He takes his hand off her ankle and puts it over her hand on the rail of the step, and doesn’t say the funny thing he had ready about wild years in Youngstown. That one was for the first half of what she said. He answers the second half.
“You came to Mass,” he says.
“I came to look.”
“You stayed in the pew with me.”
She looks at him in the half dark. “That’s not an answer.”
“The answer was this afternoon,” he says. “This is the evidence.”
She turns her hand over under his, and keeps it there. “Your turn,” she says.

So he tells her. Not the scar, not any of the versions. Danny. That he’s the one who got out. That Danny is in a cell in Leavittsburg tonight and Jack is on a porch in California with a sunburn and a girl under his blanket, and every good thing that happens to him out here, he thinks: *Danny’s not getting this*. And there isn’t anything he can send home — no grade, no money order, nothing — that makes it come out even. He stops there.

Skye doesn’t try to fix it. She wrote his brother a letter in capitals; she doesn’t make him a speech now. She holds his hand on the step, and the radio talks low on the rail, and the sea goes on at the bottom of the street.
After a while she says, “What were you saying? In the pew. When everybody went up. Your lips were going.”
“Nonna’s prayer. For the Sundays you can’t go up.”
She’s quiet a moment.
“Teach me it.”

So he does, on a porch with no swing, line by line, with the radio low on the rail behind them. *My Jesus, I believe that You are present in the Most Holy Sacrament.* She says it back, carefully, with her eyes shut, learning it like a line. *I love You above all things, and I desire to receive You into my soul. Since I cannot at this moment receive You sacramentally, come at least spiritually into my heart. I embrace You as if You were already there, and unite myself wholly to You. Never permit me to be separated from You. Amen.*

She says it back to him from the top, and gets it wrong in two places and right in the rest. *Since I can’t right now*, she says, for *Since I cannot at this moment*; and at the end, *never let me be separated from You*. But *I embrace You as if You were already there* she gets exactly, word for word, and stops after it before she goes on.

He doesn’t correct her. *Quale ti fa pregare?* Nonna asked him on Christmas night, over her beads. Three hours ago, out past the white water, he gave the answer its name. Now the answer is under his blanket on a porch on Del Playa, saying it back to him not quite right.

“Amen,” Skye says, and opens her eyes. “Next Sunday you go up. I am not going to be the reason you sit in a pew two Sundays running.” She tips her head onto his shoulder. “Once is a scandal. Twice is a pattern.”

The radio voice starts to climb. Three doors down the party goes quiet all at once, and Jack can hear the play coming through the broadcast behind it, the voice going faster and faster, and then the house groans, a long dropping groan — and turns, in the middle of it, into a scream, a living room full of people screaming, and a name comes down Del Playa from three houses away before the radio on the rail can get it out.
*Porter*.

The screen door bangs. Tomás comes out with his hair standing up and turns the radio up, and the man on it is saying overtime, and saying it again, and the street hasn’t stopped shouting. Tomás stands at the rail with his hand on the radio, looking at Jack.

journal.title: Skye Callender
journal.text: Skye Callender, two Ls. Wouldn’t give me a last name — said *Out* — till she texted it to me on the floor in Denver. Met her in a window seat in Montecito, reading O’Connor for a part and had the grandmother exactly backwards. Acts — since she was eleven. Starts here in January: spring, undeclared. She’s declared enough, she says. Doesn’t drink where there are phones. Drives a dented ’91 Saab she says is Swedish. It’s GM. Walked into the Pacific in November like it was a bath, and dared me in after her in my clothes. Asked to kiss me — out loud. She was the one who stopped, in the grandmother’s voice. Typed herself into my phone as SKYE (MISFIT), and called herself from it. Took ten hours to answer my correction. Work, she said — a carpet and a wall. Her car’s an orphan now, and it’s my fault. Nearly three hours at the Starlite, a truck stop up the 101, with Nonna’s pie on the table. Cast me as the Bible salesman. Wanted to know what believing is like — not what I believe. Wants me to miss her a reasonable amount. Get the window, she said. Kissed me again against the Saab in the lot. Slower. On purpose. She was the one who stopped — her thumb on my mouth. She’s on TV. *Sweetwater*, Thursdays at nine: she plays Cassidy, the nice one. Gina screamed. I explained GM to her. In her own car. Thanksgiving: texted me the whole drive from Pittsburgh. Spent it at her mother’s place in Studio City; the parrot says ‘momager.’ Told me not to watch her show. Wants me to be specific. We’re friends on Facebook now — one mutual friend: Theo, who knows everybody. Saturday night she called. Three hours on the porch. Made me do my family. Asked what Advent is. Asked if the TV part matters. Fell asleep in the middle of the Madonna. Monday she drove two hours from LA to sit in a car with me for two more, and set an alarm so she’d leave. Watched the President with the sound off and read his face like a script. Her phone learned a trick in September; she’s still not over it. Gives every truck on the 101 a whole life in three sentences. Knows every word of ‘Thunder Road.’ The tape deck finally let go of *Rumours*. Invited me to LA; I work Saturdays. Doesn’t take people home. Saturday, in daylight, on a rock above the tide pools: fractions, for the placement test. I drew her a pie. Sharks were a lie. I told her a saint broke in. Drove me to Burbank in the rain to be her cousin from Ohio. Everybody on a set wants something from her; she smiles for every phone. Plays a preacher’s daughter who forgives a thief. She played it dry. Washed a borrowed dress in a laundromat at one in the morning; it lived. Thinks the Immaculate Conception is the other one. Took the math test with forty kids and nobody looked at her once. Doesn’t take people home. Took me home. Lives on Del Playa, in a house with a darkroom she isn’t allowed in and two boards under the porch the boys won’t let on the rack — she’ll live there in January. On her bed I said no. She stopped everything and asked me why, and we talked till it got light. I told her it’s a no right now. She said she can work with that. Picked my present for the church party: a Magic 8-Ball. Every answer’s a line reading, she says. Her car died in Buellton; I pushed. She’s seen Our Lady of Guadalupe on every taco truck in the Valley and thought she was a brand. Friday night she took my ‘right now’ apart, point by point, with visual aids, and made a very good case. It’s still right now. I said no again, and she stopped right there and nowhere else. Came to the Anchor in my shirt; Gloria rated her boysenberry. She’s going to ask every day, she says. It’s in her calendar. Slept at her house. Just slept. She says that doesn’t happen. Taught me to surf at Ellery on Gaudete Sunday. I’m terrible. I go home in six days. She isn’t counting. Played Hale in her car from my description. Made me answer the question I couldn’t at the Starlite. Thursday at one in the morning, no moon at all, she drove the bluff with the lights off. Not before Christmas, she said — Christmas and New Year’s and long distance are too much for something new. When I get back we’re dating. Officially. A whole thing. She counted. GM is killing Saab. I’m on the hook. Christmas week: Theo’s known her since they were eleven — his father’s company makes her show. She calls him Ted; nobody else does. She saw us walk into the Hallorans’ together and hid behind a ficus. “Peace mission” was for him. He ran into her at a party in the hills on the twenty-second, and she says he knows. She had me do the weather barefoot in the snow. Seventeen days; she’s not counting. Christmas morning my family found her — Gina gave me her show on DVD. They know her as the nice one. She wants it on her headstone. The day after Christmas my whole family watched season two of her show. She was eighteen, in a blazer, on a dock. She’s good — Dad said so, and she says nobody says good. Nonna prays for Cassidy now. She bought Chesterton used on Ventura without knowing it was my book, and wants to know who picked midnight. The Monday after Christmas she called, and we talked till my phone died. New Year’s Eve she watched my ball drop on the East Coast feed at nine her time and texted, so she’d be at midnight with me. Then she had her own, at three in the morning mine, from a locked den in the hills. I told her I called Ted *Ted*. She says he’s right: that one’s hers. She has my flight home written on her hand. She read Matthew 2 because I said Sunday was Epiphany; Herod is a jealous showrunner. OFFICIALLY, in eyeliner, on a sign at the rope at Santa Barbara, in sunglasses at night. A girl from my flight filmed it, and by morning it was on a gossip blog. Skye put the still on her own Facebook herself. Her people wanted lunch: her mother, Debbie, who manages her, and her publicist, Corinne. The rules: no pictures, ‘a friend from school,’ February. Take the airport down. She took it down. There was a folder with my last name on it, and she pushed it back without opening it. At a gas station in Buellton she took the first picture of the two of us herself, at arm’s length, and put it up instead. Then she changed her status herself and made me say yes to it on her phone — the first thing anybody ever watched her do that nobody wrote. Monday she came to the Fishbowl and argued with me about a rose. My pie got her out of remedial math. Tuesday she taught me stick in an empty lot — a voice for every stall. I do a bad Frank. We argued Conan. She posted a picture of me stalling. The radio, at 2:31: Haiti. At midnight she took the picture down — not for Corinne. Wednesday in the Brick she explained the plates under Haiti from her Oceanography book, read me Milton off the front of *Frankenstein*, and fell asleep on my shoulder. At the Haiti table she borrowed Becca’s apron and was Cassidy for twenty dollars a name, and asked me where God was at 4:53. Met Laney. Met everybody. Corinne wanted a statement; she told her the girl at the table was right about the pictures, and hung up. That night she asked me to say one for them, from her. ‘Saturday.’ Thursday Margot interviewed her at the Anchor; she says I’m the same in every room. Saturday at dawn she taught me again, inside the Point. Still very bad at it. She posted it and kept it up. She came to Sully’s and learned the Who Dat. Laney took a shot at her; she had it handled, she says, and I didn’t let her finish, and she says she’ll reward that sort of behavior. In the Saab I told her some about Lena — that we were close in the fall. She said she can tell there’s a rest. She drove me to confession, and went back to Sully’s without me. Saturday night she read me Sunday’s Gospel off her phone. Three nights in LA: a fitting for the wedding episode — she’s not the bride, she checked. Tuesday she made me explain Massachusetts while I walked. The tornado took Sol’s swing. Wednesday she drove home with the top down in the rain and put the two of us up on Facebook, soaked. Thursday we argued the Supreme Court under one umbrella until it turned inside out. She’s been a corporation since she was twelve — Skylark Pictures; her mother named it. She wrote my brother, in capitals; Rudy says write the number big. Friday the sun came out, and she called the telethon as Skylark. Saturday she drove six hours to the Walk for Life, walked the whole thing arguing with me, and stood in front of Clare when a man started screaming. Sunday she came to Mass. I told her why I didn’t go up. Out past the break I told her what I know about the basement, which isn’t much, and about Nonna’s question and Danny’s. She’s the answer to both. She knows there’s more; she said that’s enough. She asked me to teach her Nonna’s prayer.

response: Tomás looks at him a moment longer, and turns it off, and takes it inside with him.
The porch is quiet. Skye’s head stays on his shoulder. For twenty minutes there’s only the sea at the bottom of the street, and the party three doors down going up and down without them.

The street tells him anyway. It goes off all at once — horns up and down Del Playa, somebody banging a pot with a spoon, the party coming out onto its lawn with its arms in the air, a girl on a balcony yelling *WHO DAT* at the ocean. He doesn’t get up. He sits on the top step with Skye against him while it goes by.
Tomás puts his head out of the screen door. “Who dat, bro,” he says, and goes back in.
Tomás leaves it, and stays at the rail with his hand on top of the radio.

The Saints win the toss. Jack listens to the rest of it with Skye’s hand in his under the blanket: the drive, the voice going up and coming down, the field goal unit going out. The party three doors down has gone silent. Skye’s fingers tighten on his. The snap. The hold. The man’s voice going up, and up, and breaking.

And the street goes off all at once — horns, a pot, the party out on its lawn, somebody running down the middle of Del Playa with a flag. He doesn’t get up. He sits where he is with her hand in his and the street going past the end of the steps.
“Who dat, bro,” Tomás says quietly, to Jack, and turns it down.

Skye sits up and holds out her hands, and Tomás puts the radio in them. She sets it on her knees and puts her ear to the speaker and her face goes completely blank, a pro’s face, a girl who has been told when to react for a living, and she listens to overtime like that, giving him nothing. The toss. The drive. She keeps her face. Three doors down the party has stopped breathing.

At the kick she’s on her feet with the radio over her head, and she calls it — in a sportscaster’s voice, deep, from somewhere in her chest, hand at her ear like a man in a booth — forty yards, it’s good, it’s *good*, New Orleans is going to the Super Bowl — as the street goes off around her: horns, pots, the party pouring out onto its lawn.
Jack doesn’t get up. He sits on the top step and watches her do it.
“Who dat, bro,” Tomás says, and takes his radio back.
